sections.h: The martyrs' "atoning death" in 4 Maccabees
sections.b: 4 Maccabees says that the martyrs under Antiochus "became, as it were, a life in exchange for the nation's sin. Through the blood of those godly people and their atoning death, divine providence saved Israel" (4 Maccabees 17:22). The key words are antipsychon, "a life in exchange", and hilasterios, "atoning"; in Codex Sinaiticus the second is the noun hilasterion, the word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25. Scholars disagree on how the two passages relate: Jarvis J. Williams, according to the publisher's description of his book, argues that Maccabean martyr theology significantly influenced Paul's view of Jesus' death, while Daniel Bailey argues that the noun means different things in each and that the martyrs are not compared with sacrificial victims, the atonement lid in Romans and a Greek votive offering in 4 Maccabees. The book is not Scripture for most churches (see its opening pages). Whether faithful people's sufferings can help atone for others is asked on the card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38.
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 17:20-22; 4 Maccabees 6:28-29; Romans 3:25; Mark 10:45; 2 Maccabees 7:37-38; Isaiah 53:12

uncommon: Some scholars read the Sinaiticus text of 4 Maccabees 17:22 as calling the martyrs' death a votive offering to God, a Greek image, not a temple sacrifice.

sections.h: The martyr as athlete (4 Maccabees 17)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees pictures the deaths of Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother as a contest in the Greek games: "Virtue was the judge who gave out the prizes", the prize was "incorruption", "The tyrant was their opponent", the world looked on, and "The fear of God won, and she crowned her own athletes" (4 Maccabees 17:12-15). The New Testament uses the same pictures of crown and race for faithful endurance (2 Timothy 4:7-8; Hebrews 12:1-2; Revelation 2:10), and Christian martyr stories took them over. The mother calls her sons to the contest "to testify on behalf of the nation" (4 Maccabees 16:16), language on the way to the Christian word "martyr".
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 17:11-16; 4 Maccabees 16:16; 2 Timothy 4:7-8; Hebrews 12:1-2; Revelation 2:10; 1 Corinthians 9:24-25

sections.h: The mother of the seven in 4 Maccabees 14-18
sections.b: 4 Maccabees gives most of its last five chapters to the mother. Her love for her sons is drawn as strong as nature can make it (4 Maccabees 14:13-20); she holds "two votes" in the council of her soul and votes with Abraham (4 Maccabees 15:25-28); she is "mother of the nation, defender of the law" (4 Maccabees 15:29). She urges her sons in Hebrew during Eleazar's torture (4 Maccabees 16:15-23) and, the guards said, threw herself onto the pyre so that no one would touch her (4 Maccabees 17:1). A second speech recalls her girlhood and the Scriptures her husband taught their sons (4 Maccabees 18:6-19). Later tradition gave her names: Solomonia in the Orthodox lives of the saints, Solomona in Erasmus's Latin paraphrase and Hannah in the medieval Hebrew history Yosippon, as Townshend (1913) reports for the last two.

sections.h: Pure and immortal souls (4 Maccabees)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees hopes for the soul's life with God at death and never mentions the resurrection of the body. The brothers run "on the road to immortality" (4 Maccabees 14:5); their mother bears them again "into immortality" (4 Maccabees 16:13); they "now stand beside God's throne" (4 Maccabees 17:18); and at the end they are gathered with their mother "in the place of their fathers" (4 Maccabees 18:23), having received from God souls that are pure and immortal. In 18:23 the word "immortal" is a correction in two of the three codices. 2 Maccabees tells the same deaths with a hope of bodily resurrection (2 Maccabees 7:9, 14).
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 14:5-6; 4 Maccabees 16:13; 4 Maccabees 17:12; 4 Maccabees 17:18; 4 Maccabees 18:23; 2 Maccabees 7:9; Wisdom of Solomon 3:1-4

sections.h: A martyr book without the resurrection
sections.b: 4 Maccabees retells the martyrdoms of 2 Maccabees 6-7 but leaves out their hope of rising again. Where the mother in 2 Maccabees trusts that the Creator "will give you back the breath and the life in his mercy" (2 Maccabees 7:23), the mother in 4 Maccabees bears her sons "into immortality" (4 Maccabees 16:13). The only hint of resurrection is the father's teaching of Ezekiel's question, "Will these dry bones live?" (4 Maccabees 18:17), in a passage whose place in the book is debated.

sections.h: Welcomed by the fathers (4 Maccabees)
sections.b: The brothers expect that "we will be received by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" (4 Maccabees 13:17), and the book ends with them "gathered together in the place of their fathers" (4 Maccabees 18:23). They "now stand beside God's throne" (4 Maccabees 17:18), and those who die for God "live to God" (4 Maccabees 16:25). The pictures are close to Abraham's embrace in Luke 16:22 and the souls before the throne in Revelation 6:9-11 and 7:15.
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 13:17; 4 Maccabees 16:25; 4 Maccabees 17:18; 4 Maccabees 18:23; Luke 16:22; Luke 20:38; Revelation 6:9-11

sections.h: Isaac and the mother of seven (4 Maccabees)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees makes the binding of Isaac its model for martyrdom. Isaac "was willing to be slaughtered for godliness" (4 Maccabees 13:12), going beyond Genesis 22, which tells only what Abraham did. The mother "had a soul like Abraham's" (4 Maccabees 14:20), and she reminds her sons that "our father Abraham hurried to slaughter his son Isaac, the father of our nation" (4 Maccabees 16:20). Their father had read to them of "Isaac, offered as a whole burnt offering" (4 Maccabees 18:11). Her test is set beside Abraham's: he gave up one son, she seven.
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 13:12; 4 Maccabees 14:20; 4 Maccabees 15:28; 4 Maccabees 16:20; 4 Maccabees 18:11; Genesis 22:1-19; Hebrews 11:17-19

sections.h: The mother on the pyre (4 Maccabees 17:1)
sections.b: 2 Maccabees says only that the mother died last (2 Maccabees 7:41). 4 Maccabees adds the guards' report that she "flung herself onto the pyre, so that no one would touch any part of her body" (4 Maccabees 17:1); the youngest son also threw himself onto the braziers (4 Maccabees 12:20). Jewish tradition told the same end: in the Talmud's story of the woman and her seven sons, "She too in the end went up to the roof, fell, and died" (Bavli Gittin 57b, William Davidson translation on Sefaria), and she is praised. Townshend (1913) notes that the Hebrew Bible nowhere forbids such an act and that 2 Maccabees honors Razis's death (2 Maccabees 14:41-46). Christian writers judged such deaths with care. Augustine held that killing oneself breaks the commandment against killing, yet would not condemn women of the persecutions honored by the church, allowing that they may have acted by God's prompting (City of God 1.26). Gregory of Nazianzus, as Townshend reports, praised the mother for running to the pyre as to a bridal bed.

sections.h: Ruling the passions, not uprooting them (4 Maccabees 13-16)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees uses Stoic words, reason "master in its own right" and "sovereign" over the passions (4 Maccabees 13:1; 16:1), but not the Stoic goal. The Stoics taught that the virtuous person feels no passions. In 4 Maccabees the seven brothers love one another deeply (4 Maccabees 13:19-27) and the mother loves her sons more than any mother (4 Maccabees 15:4-10); their reason masters that love without destroying it. The book had said so earlier: reason is not the uprooter of the passions but their opponent (4 Maccabees 3:5).

sections.h: A daughter of Abraham (4 Maccabees)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees calls the mother of seven "a daughter of Abraham" (4 Maccabees 15:28), "Abraham's daughter" (4 Maccabees 18:20), and her sons "Abraham's children" (4 Maccabees 18:23). Her faith is Abraham's "God-fearing steadfastness" at the binding of Isaac. Luke gives the same title to a woman Jesus heals: "this woman, a daughter of Abraham" (Luke 13:16).
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 15:28; 4 Maccabees 17:6; 4 Maccabees 18:1; 4 Maccabees 18:20; 4 Maccabees 18:23; Luke 13:16

sections.h: The mother's roll call (4 Maccabees 16; 18)
sections.b: The mother of the seven gives two lists of heroes, like Hebrews 11: Abraham and Isaac, Daniel among the lions, and Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael in the furnace (4 Maccabees 16:20-21); then Abel, Isaac, Joseph in prison, Phinehas, the three in the fire and Daniel, with words of Isaiah, David, Solomon, Ezekiel and Moses (4 Maccabees 18:11-19). Almost all are righteous sufferers. The book also says the martyrs died "fixing their eyes on God" (4 Maccabees 17:10), the same Greek verb Hebrews uses for fixing our eyes on Jesus (Hebrews 12:2).
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 16:20-21; 4 Maccabees 17:10; 4 Maccabees 18:11-19; Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 11:17-19; Hebrews 11:33-38; Hebrews 12:1-2; 1 Maccabees 2:51-60

sections.h: The three as models in 4 Maccabees
sections.b: The seven brothers cheer one another: "Let us copy the three young men" who looked down on the furnace (4 Maccabees 13:9). The mother names Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, flung into the furnace, among those who "endured for God" (4 Maccabees 16:21), and their father taught them the story (4 Maccabees 18:12), with Isaiah's promise for those who walk through fire (4 Maccabees 18:14; Isaiah 43:2). Unlike the three, the brothers are not rescued; the book admires the endurance, not the rescue.
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 13:9; 4 Maccabees 16:3; 4 Maccabees 16:21; 4 Maccabees 18:12; 4 Maccabees 18:14; Daniel 3:1-30; Isaiah 43:2

sections.h: The martyrs' blood (4 Maccabees 17:22)
sections.b: "Through the blood of those godly people and their atoning death, divine providence saved Israel" (4 Maccabees 17:22). The book applies to martyrs the law's teaching that blood makes atonement (Leviticus 17:11), as the New Testament applies it to Christ (Romans 3:25; 5:9).

sections.h: Brotherly love and a mother's love (4 Maccabees 13-15)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees gives a long account of family love. The seven brothers shared a womb, blood, milk and schooling in God's law, so their philadelphia, brotherly love, was strong (4 Maccabees 13:19-27). The mother's love was stronger still, planted by seven pregnancies (4 Maccabees 15:4-10), and the speaker compares it with birds and bees defending their young (4 Maccabees 14:13-19). The book's point is that godliness ruled even these loves, not that they were wrong; it calls the brothers' love "even more precious to them" because of godliness (4 Maccabees 13:26).

sections.h: Taught at home (4 Maccabees 18:18)
sections.b: The mother of the seven remembers that their father "did not forget the song that Moses taught", with its words "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39), which she gives in the future tense: "I will kill, and I will make alive" (4 Maccabees 18:18). In 2 Maccabees the brothers quote the same song (2 Maccabees 7:6).

sections.h: The tyrant punished in life and after death (4 Maccabees 18)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees says Antiochus "has been punished on earth, and now that he is dead he is still being punished" (4 Maccabees 18:5), and that "divine Justice has gone after the accursed man and will go after him still" (4 Maccabees 18:22). 2 Maccabees 9 tells his painful death; 4 Maccabees adds punishment after death, as the brothers had warned him (4 Maccabees 9:9; 12:12).

sections.h: "The rib that was built" (4 Maccabees 18:7-8)
sections.b: The mother of the seven says she "guarded the rib that was built", her body as a woman, in the words of the Greek of Genesis 2:22, where God "built" the rib into a woman. Unlike Eve, she says, "The destroyer who deceives, the snake, did not spoil the purity of my virginity" (4 Maccabees 18:8; compare Genesis 3:13; 2 Corinthians 11:3).

sections.h: A tree of life for those who do his will
sections.b: 4 Maccabees quotes Proverbs 3:18 in a form of its own: "It is a tree of life to all who do his will" (4 Maccabees 18:16). Proverbs, in Hebrew and Greek, speaks of those who hold on to wisdom; the quotation turns wisdom into obedience.

sections.h: The martyrs' games (4 Maccabees 17): Greek, not Roman
sections.b: A Jewish speech of the first or early second century AD pictures martyrdom as the Greek athletic games (the agon), not the Roman arena: a judge who gives the prizes, a first round, an opponent, a watching world and a crown (4 Maccabees 17:11-16). Townshend (1913) took this freedom with Greek imagery as a sign that the writer lived in a Greek city.

sections.h: The proof from love (4 Maccabees 13-18)
sections.b: After each proof the speech repeats its thesis: "godly reason is master in its own right over the passions" (4 Maccabees 13:1), and "godly reason is sovereign over the passions" (4 Maccabees 16:1). Both verses begin with "if": if the brothers, and then even an old mother, endured to the end, the thesis stands. In these chapters the passion overcome is love itself: the brothers' love for one another (4 Maccabees 13:19-27) and a mother's love for her sons (4 Maccabees 15:4-10). Reason rules these loves without destroying them. The closing appeal states the thesis once more (4 Maccabees 18:2).

sections.h: The seven brothers' virtues (4 Maccabees 15:10)
sections.b: The speaker says of the seven brothers, "They were just, self-restrained and courageous" (4 Maccabees 15:10): three of the four virtues defined at the start of the speech (4 Maccabees 1:2-4, 18). He adds that they were great-souled, loved their brothers and loved their mother, and that they showed it by keeping the law. The Greek virtues and the law of Moses are learned together.
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 15:10; 4 Maccabees 1:2-4; 4 Maccabees 1:18; Wisdom of Solomon 8:7

sections.h: The revolt credited to the martyrs (4 Maccabees 17-18)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees never tells the war of Judas Maccabeus. It sums up the result in one verse and credits it to the martyrs: "Through them the nation had peace. It brought back the rule of good law in the homeland and drove the enemy out by siege" (4 Maccabees 18:4). Their deaths were the turning point (4 Maccabees 17:20-22), as in 2 Maccabees, where after the martyrs "the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy" (2 Maccabees 8:5).

sections.h: Greek images in a Jewish speech (4 Maccabees 13-18)
sections.b: The second half of 4 Maccabees is full of Greek culture put to the service of the law: the Sirens and the swan's song (4 Maccabees 15:21), the soul as a city council voting with pebbles (4 Maccabees 15:25-26), a painter's picture of the martyrs (4 Maccabees 17:7), and the athletic games with their judge, contestants, spectators and crown (4 Maccabees 17:11-16). Townshend (1913) took this freedom with Greek images as a sign that the writer lived in a Greek city, and he thought of Alexandria.

sections.h: The martyrs and the suffering servant (4 Maccabees 17:22)
sections.b: Isaiah's servant "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). 4 Maccabees does not quote Isaiah 53, but it applies the same pattern to the martyrs: "They became, as it were, a life in exchange for the nation's sin" (4 Maccabees 17:22). Readers who see a link point to the shared idea of a righteous death for others; the words themselves differ, and the book names no servant. The New Testament applies the pattern to Christ.
